newsitem.title: USA: Exponential closes Silicon Valley operation, fires 40.
newsitem.headline: Exponential closes Silicon Valley operation, fires 40.

text.p: Exponential Technology Inc., whose speedy computer chips were viewed as central to Apple Computer Inc.'s turnaround plan, closed its Silicon Valley operation and fired 40 employees, citing lack of money.
The closely held company also dropped development of the X704 chip, its chief product, said Rick Bergman, vice president of marketing.
The company has a design centre in Austin, Texas, where 30 engineers will continue to work on undisclosed products, Bergman said.
Exponential, based in San Jose, Calif., was developing a turbo-charged version of the PowerPC microprocessor, the chip that serves as the brain of Apple's Macintosh computers.

Exponential ran into trouble, however, because the X704 microprocessor was not much faster than upcoming versions of the PowerPC, a chip jointly designed by Apple, Motorola Inc. and International Business Machines Corp.

Apple itself was Exponential's biggest investor. The struggling computer maker had hoped Exponential could develop a super-fast chip to gives Macs an advantage over PCs that use Pentium chips from Intel Corp.

Earlier this week, however, Apple executives said at a developers conference that they did not plan to use Exponential's chips in any upcoming products because prototypes of Exponential chips were only slightly faster than PowerPC chips in the works.
Last week, Exponential fired 25 percent of its workers to conserve cash while it looked for more investors.
Apple's decision not to use the X704 "certainly was a factor" in the decision to stop its development, Bergman said.
The company will continue to develop other products, Bergman said, but declined to say what they are.
Exponential had raised $27 million from investors, including Apple and venture capitalists Nazem & Co., Woodside Fund and Venrock Associates.
